components.topic: 💬 Code Review Roundtable: How Closures Capture Variables and Their Lifecycle

messages.content: Priya, I was doing a code review and found a coworker's for loop that registers three setTimeouts — but they all print the same value, 3, instead of the expected 0, 1, 2. What's going on?

That's the classic closure trap. Variables declared with var don't have block scope, so the entire for loop shares a single i variable. All three callbacks "close over" a reference to that same i — by the time the setTimeouts fire, the loop has long since finished, and i is now 3.
So a closure captures a reference to the variable itself, not the value at that moment? If I want each callback to remember its own i, what should I do?

Two common fixes: option one, swap var for let — let has block scope, so every loop iteration creates a brand-new binding for i. Option two, use an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) to create a fresh local scope on each iteration and pass the current i in as an argument, forcing a value copy.
So what let really does is give each loop iteration its own independent lexical environment, and each closure captures a different one?

Exactly right! That's the essence of a closure: a function plus the lexical environment it was defined in. let gives each iteration its own independent lexical environment, so the three closures are all independent — naturally printing 0, 1, 2.

components.title: Closure: A Function Bound to Its Lexical Environment
components.definition: A closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment it was defined in. Even after the outer function has returned, the inner function can still access and mutate variables from the outer function's scope — those variables aren't garbage-collected; they're "sealed" inside the closure and stay alive.

components.title: Mental Model for Closures: A Backpack and a Lexical Environment
components.description: The key to understanding closures: a function isn't just a block of executable code — it also carries a "backpack" with it, the lexical environment it was defined in. That backpack holds references to every variable from the outer scope.
components.analogy: Think of a closure as an explorer traveling with a personal notebook: no matter where this explorer goes (wherever the function gets called), their notebook (the lexical environment) always travels with them. What's written in the notebook isn't "a snapshot of the variables at departure" — it's "the address of the variable itself." If the variable gets changed, the next time they flip the notebook open, they see the latest value.

pillars.title: Lexical Scope
pillars.description: JavaScript determines scope at the moment a function is defined (not when it's called). An inner function can access every variable of its outer functions, forming a scope chain.

pillars.title: Persistent Variable References
pillars.description: As long as a closure function exists, the outer variables it captured won't be garbage-collected — even after the outer function has finished executing and returned.

pillars.title: Encapsulating Private State
pillars.description: Closures are JavaScript's core mechanism for "private variables" — the enclosed variables can't be accessed or modified directly from the outside, only through the methods that are exposed.

questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Calling outer() returns the inner function and creates the lexical environment { x: 10 }.
fn is the combination of the inner function plus that closure.
• First fn(): x goes from 10 → 15, returns 15;
• Second fn(): x goes from 15 → 20, returns 20.
The key point: inner captures a reference to x, not a copy of its value — so every mutation persists.

components.title: Summary: Closures Are a Cornerstone of JavaScript's Functional Style
components.analogy:
Closures are JavaScript's core mechanism for private variables, function factories, and modular encapsulation. Understanding closures means truly understanding JavaScript's lexical scope and function execution model.
📌 Glossary

A closure is the combination of a function and its lexical scope. The outer variables a closure references aren't cleaned up by garbage collection (GC), which is how you get "private variables." The classic pitfall comes from the difference between var's function scope and let's block scope — an IIFE or let can force each iteration to get its own independent lexical environment.
